questions.question: An operator wrote the wrong date in a batch record and wants to correct it. Which approach is consistent with <1029>?

options.A: Cover it with correction fluid, write the correct date, and sign at the bottom of the page so the record can continue to be used
options.B: Leave the original entry legible, identify who made the correction and when, and add an explanation if the reason is not obvious
options.C: Tear out the page, rewrite it, and destroy the original page to avoid confusing later reviewers
options.D: Overwrite it in pencil and sign at the bottom of the page, adding the reason for the correction during batch review

questions.explanation: Any change must not obscure the original entry, and it must be traceable who made the change and when; where the reason is not obvious, it must be explained. Predefined correction codes may be used, for example WD for wrong date.
questions.reference: USP <1029> Good Documentation Guidelines › Data Collection and Recording

questions.question: A section of a paper record does not need to be completed for this operation. How should it be handled under <1029>?

options.A: Strike it through or write N/A; in an electronic system it may be left blank if who entered it and when can be traced
options.B: Always leave it blank, because an empty field shows the operation was not performed
options.C: Strike it through with a single line and have a second person sign; electronic systems may never leave fields blank
options.D: Fill it in with data from the previous batch so the page is complete, and note the batch referenced

questions.explanation: All data entry fields should be completed, and unused portions struck through with a single line and/or "N/A"; in an electronic system where who completed each field and when can be traced, fields may be left blank. Filling in data from another batch is an improper record.
questions.reference: USP <1029> Good Documentation Guidelines › Data Collection and Recording

questions.question: What is the minimum baseline <1029> sets for the retention period of GMP records?

options.A: 1 year from the batch manufacturing date, regardless of the batch expiry date, after which records may be destroyed
options.B: 5 years from batch release, after which all records must be destroyed and no copy may be kept
options.C: 10 years after the product is marketed, extendable only if the regulatory authority notifies otherwise
options.D: It depends on regulations or company procedures, but at least 1 year after the batch expiry date

questions.explanation: The retention period depends on regulatory requirements or company procedures, but must be at least 1 year past the batch expiration date; an appropriate record retention and archiving policy should be established, and records must remain legible throughout the retention period.
questions.reference: USP <1029> Good Documentation Guidelines › Different Types of GMP Documents › Retention of Documents

questions.question: Which statement about the relationship between the Master Batch Record (MBR) and the Executed Batch Record is correct?

options.A: They are the same document, renamed by the quality unit at batch release
options.B: The MBR is the template for a specific product, and the Executed Batch Record documents a given batch against it
options.C: The Executed Batch Record is the template, and the MBR is used to record actual data for the batch
options.D: The MBR records only test results, and the Executed Batch Record records only cleaning status

questions.explanation: The MBR is the template for manufacturing a specific product; the Executed Batch Record is based on the MBR and documents the steps and materials for one batch of production, and should be approved by an appropriate representative of the manufacturing or packaging site. The other options reverse or confuse the two roles.
questions.reference: USP <1029> Good Documentation Guidelines › Different Types of GMP Documents › Batch Records

questions.question: Under <1029>, which section appears only in a report and not in the content of a protocol?

options.A: Predefined acceptance criteria used to judge whether results meet the specified requirements
options.B: Purpose, explaining why the activity is performed and its intended objective
options.C: Assessment or evaluation, stating the conclusions drawn from the results
options.D: Review and approval, signed by appropriate personnel

questions.explanation: Both protocols and reports include purpose, plan or description, predefined acceptance criteria, review and approval, and revision history; references to deviations or investigations, assessment or evaluation, and data references appear only in reports.
questions.reference: USP <1029> Good Documentation Guidelines › Different Types of GMP Documents › Protocols and Reports
